# German cross-border electricity balance

Did Germany pay more for imported electricity than it earned from exports? This
values every cross-border flow at day-ahead prices, per border and per market
time unit, and reports it over a day or a range.

```
de_trade_balance.py    the analysis and CLI report
build_data.py          reshapes a range into data/<month>.json + data/index.json
data/                  the generated series, one file per calendar month
index.html             the dashboard, one file, no dependencies
serve.py               serves it locally, bound to localhost
```

## Quick start

```bash
pip install pandas requests           # entsoe-py too, for --source entsoe
./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-08-16          # one day, per MTU
./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-08-16 --source smard   # gross per-direction flows
./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-07             # all of July, per day
./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026 --by week      # the year, per ISO week
./de_trade_balance.py --demo                     # synthetic, no network
```

No account needed for either no-auth source. Raw responses are cached under
`~/.cache/de_trade_balance`, which matters most for energy-charts: it is rate
limited per IP and endpoint and has no bulk export, so a cold month of all 11
borders costs ~90s, then is free forever. SMARD is far cheaper — it takes many
series per request, so a month of every border plus prices and load is six
requests in a couple of seconds.

## The dashboard

```bash
python3 build_data.py --date 2026-07-18 --days 30   # fill data/ (SMARD)
./serve.py                                          # then open localhost:8731
```

`index.html` and `data/` both sit at the root, so the page's relative fetches work
the same locally as when published and there is no dev-only path. `serve.py` is a
thin wrapper on the stdlib server that binds to localhost — `http.server` otherwise
listens on every interface, which would hand `.git` to anyone on the network — and
refuses dotted paths for the same reason.

`build_data.py` upserts by date, so re-running a day corrects it in place. Both
sources revise the last few days after first publication, which is why the daily
job re-fetches a short trailing window rather than only yesterday.

Data is written one file per calendar month plus an `index.json` manifest. The page
reads the manifest first, then fetches only the months its range needs — a 30-day
view pulls two files (~140 KB) rather than the whole history, and switching to a
longer range fetches just the months it is missing. Reference price levels live in
`data/reference_prices.json`, hand-refreshed.

### Publishing it

Settings → Pages → Source: **GitHub Actions**. The workflow assembles the publish
directory from `index.html` plus `data/` and uploads it — that is what frees the repo
layout, since branch-based Pages can only serve `/` or `/docs` and would drag
everything the page fetches into one of them. Publishing only those two also keeps
the scripts and git history out of the served site. There is still no build step and
no CDN: the page is one HTML file with inline SVG charts and no dependencies.

`.github/workflows/daily.yml` refreshes the data every morning, commits it, and
deploys.
**GitHub only fires `schedule` on the default branch**, so while this sits on a
side branch the cron will not run — trigger it by hand from the Actions tab
(`workflow_dispatch`, optionally with a date range to backfill), or merge this
branch to make the cron live.

## Which source to use

**SMARD** (`--source smard`, the dashboard default). Bundesnetzagentur publishes it
under a statutory mandate (§ 111d EnWG) and grants
[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) in its own right, and it
carries each direction of each border separately. It is the only source that is both
publishable and complete — cross-checked against ENTSO-E for 2026-07-18, all 11
borders and both directions, agreeing to under 0.02 GWh. No account needed.

The other two are worth keeping for what they are: **`--source entsoe`** as an
independent cross-check (free token in `ENTSOE_API_TOKEN`, `pip install entsoe-py`),
and **`--source energy-charts`** as a no-fuss fallback with a finer generation-type
taxonomy.

| Source | licence to republish | flows | Denmark |
|---|---|---|---|
| smard | CC BY 4.0 granted by BNetzA under § 111d EnWG | gross per direction | DK_1 / DK_2 split |
| energy-charts | CC BY 4.0 (prices from SMARD) | netted, ~27% low | often unsplit |
| entsoe | prices + scheduled exchanges **not** on the free-re-use list | gross per direction | split |

That last row is the constraint that shapes everything. The dashboard *republishes*,
and ENTSO-E's
[list of data available for free re-use](https://transparencyplatform.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/40921911218961-Legal-Terms-and-Conditions)
(Article 2.5 of its terms) does not cover the two series this project leans on:

| Series | Article | On the free-re-use list |
|---|---|---|
| Physical flows | 12.1.g | yes, item #18 |
| Day-ahead prices | 12.1.d | **no** |

The whole `12.1.d/e/f` market-results block is absent. That is not an oversight:
those series belong to the power exchanges rather than the TSOs, and ENTSO-E cannot
sub-license what it does not hold rights to. The transparency mandate makes the
data *visible*; it does not grant redistribution.

SMARD carries the same series and licenses them openly, which is why the published
page uses it. Worth being precise about why that works, because it is not that SMARD
is upstream of ENTSO-E — it isn't. SMARD states plainly that it takes its data
*from* ENTSO-E. But Bundesnetzagentur publishes under its own statutory mandate
(§ 111d EnWG) and grants CC BY 4.0 as licensor, so ENTSO-E is the delivery channel
rather than the licensor, and Article 2.5 — which binds Transparency Platform data
users — is not the instrument that governs data taken from SMARD. Attribution must
read exactly **"Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de"**.

(energy-charts' non-SMARD bidding zones are marked private/internal use only, so
don't widen `NEIGHBOURS` and then publish.) The ENTSO-E list checked was the
18 Oct 2023 revision, which does get amended.

Measured over July 2026, the two agree on `balance_at_de_price` to **0.0002%** and
on `congestion_rent` to 0.6% — not luck, but because both reduce to net-only
expressions per MTU:

```
balance_at_de_price = sum(net_MWh * price_de)
congestion_rent     = sum(net_MWh * spread)
```

so a source that reports flows already netted cannot shift either. What it does
shift is everything gross: energy-charts nets opposite flows within a border-hour,
so `import_gwh`/`export_gwh` come out ~26% low, and the volume-weighted prices are
biased apart. It also does not carry DK_2 — though the Kontek energy is still
there, filed under DK_1, so only the zonal pricing suffers.

## Reading the numbers

There is no single true figure, so three are reported. Cross-border trade in the
coupled day-ahead market is *implicit*: nobody buys a labelled MWh from France.
German buyers pay the German price, the seller abroad receives theirs, and the
difference is congestion rent collected by the transmission operators on both
sides — regulated back into grid fees and interconnector investment, not a loss.

Day-ahead only: intraday and balancing trades settle at other prices and are not
included. The long-form version of all of this is the docstring at the top of
`de_trade_balance.py`.

## Attribution

Cross-border exchange, day-ahead prices and load come from
[Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de](https://www.smard.de) under
[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Under
`--source energy-charts` the prices are the same SMARD series redistributed
unchanged by [Energy-Charts.info](https://www.energy-charts.info) (Fraunhofer ISE),
which is then also the source of the exchange series; its other bidding zones are
marked private/internal use only, so don't widen the border list and then publish.
The dashboard's footer credits whichever source each day actually came from.

SMARD's download API is undocumented, so the parts worth knowing are recorded in
`SmardBackend`: the module manifest lives at
`/app/chart_configuration/market_data_configuration.json`, cross-border modules
exist only for region `DE-LU`, columns must be matched by header label rather than
request order, and imports arrive negative in German number format.

211	def example_day(backend, outdir: str, start, end) -> None:
212	    """Write one real day, hour by hour, as a worked example of how a price happens.
213	
214	    Picks the day in the range with the widest intraday price spread, because that is
215	    the one where the mechanism is visible: the stack fills bottom-up with whatever is
216	    cheapest, and the price follows whatever had to run last. Records which day and
217	    why, so the choice is not mistaken for a hand-picked illustration.
218	    """
219	    if not hasattr(backend, "generation"):
220	        return
221	    ids = [i for v in STACK.values() for i in v]
222	    try:
223	        frames, prices = [], []
224	        for ws, we in dtb.windows(start, end, "month"):
225	            frames.append(pd.DataFrame(backend._fetch(ids, ws, we)))
226	            prices.append(backend._prices_for(ws, we)["DE_LU"])
227	        gen = pd.concat(frames).sort_index()
228	        px = pd.concat(prices).sort_index()
229	        load = pd.concat([backend.demand(ws, we)["load_mw"]
230	                          for ws, we in dtb.windows(start, end, "month")]).sort_index()
231	    except Exception as exc:
232	        print(f"  ! example day: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
233	        return
234	
235	    j = gen.join(px.rename("price"), how="inner").join(load.rename("load"), how="inner")
236	    j = j[(j.index >= start) & (j.index < end)].dropna(subset=["price"])
237	    if j.empty:
238	        return
239	    spread = j.groupby(dtb.period_of(j.index, "day"))["price"].agg(lambda s: s.max() - s.min())
240	    pick = spread.idxmax()
241	    day = j[dtb.period_of(j.index, "day") == pick]
242	
243	    LABEL = {1004068: "Photovoltaik", 1004067: "Wind Onshore", 1001225: "Wind Offshore",
244	             1001226: "Wasserkraft", 1004070: "Pumpspeicher", 1004066: "Biomasse",
245	             1001228: "Sonstige Erneuerbare", 1001223: "Braunkohle",
246	             1004069: "Steinkohle", 1004071: "Erdgas", 1001227: "Sonstige Konventionelle"}
247	    hours = []
248	    for ts, r in day.iterrows():
249	        row = {"hour": ts.strftime("%H:%M"), "price": _n(r["price"]), "load_gw": _n(r["load"] / 1000)}
250	        for bucket, mods in STACK.items():
251	            cols = [LABEL[i] for i in mods if LABEL[i] in day.columns]
252	            row[bucket] = _n(sum(r[c] for c in cols) / 1000)
253	        hours.append(row)
254	
255	    _write(os.path.join(outdir, "example_day.json"), {
256	        "date": pick,
257	        "chosen_because": (f"widest intraday price spread in the refreshed range: "
258	                           f"{spread[pick]:.0f} EUR/MWh"),
259	        "note": ("Generation is what actually ran, grouped cheap-to-dear. The ordering is "
260	                 "the conventional merit order, not observed bids -- what each unit offered "
261	                 "is not public, so the stack shows volumes, not costs."),
262	        "source": "Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de",
263	        "buckets": list(STACK),
264	        "hours": hours,

269	def wind_shortfall(backend, start, end, price: pd.Series
270	                   ) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, dict] | tuple[None, None]:
271	    """Per day: how far wind ran below its own day-ahead forecast, split by price sign.
272	
273	    Signed, never clipped. An earlier version summed max(0, forecast - actual) over
274	    negative-price hours, which is not a measure of anything: forecast error is roughly
275	    symmetric, so discarding the negative side accumulates ordinary noise into a large
276	    positive number. Over Jan-Aug it reported 781 GWh where the signed deficit was
277	    563 GWh -- a 39% inflation -- and on nine days it showed a positive "missing" bar
278	    for days when wind ran *above* forecast in exactly the hours being counted. Under a
279	    sign-flip null the clipped statistic returns ~500 GWh from pure noise, so most of
280	    what it reported was its own one-sidedness.
281	
282	    Both hour sets are carried so the page can state a like-for-like control: the same
283	    signed measure, as a share of forecast, in negative-price hours against every other
284	    hour. Comparing a clipped subset sum against a signed all-hours sum -- which the
285	    page used to do -- is what let a 32 GWh claim be "supported" by a -142 GWh control.
286	
287	    Returns the daily frame and the adjacency profile (see `adjacency`), which is the
288	    evidence that actually identifies the effect.
289	    """
290	    if not (hasattr(backend, "wind_forecast") and hasattr(backend, "generation")):
291	        return None, None
292	    fc, act = [], []
293	    for ws, we in dtb.windows(start, end, "month"):
294	        try:
295	            fc.append(backend.wind_forecast(ws, we))
296	            g = backend.generation(ws, we)
297	            act.append(g[[c for c in ("wind_onshore", "wind_offshore") if c in g]].sum(axis=1))
298	        except Exception as exc:
299	            print(f"  ! wind shortfall {ws.date()}: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
300	    if not fc or not act:
301	        return None, None
302	    j = pd.DataFrame({"fc": pd.concat(fc).sort_index(),
303	                      "act": pd.concat(act).sort_index()}).join(price.rename("px"), how="inner")
304	    j = j[(j.index >= start) & (j.index < end)].dropna(subset=["fc", "act"])
305	    if j.empty:
306	        return None, None
307	
308	    j["deficit"] = j.fc - j.act                 # signed: positive means wind ran short
309	    below = j.px < 0
310	    key = dtb.period_of(j.index, "day")
311	    daily = pd.DataFrame({
312	        "wind_forecast_gwh": j.fc.groupby(key).sum() / 1000,
313	        "wind_actual_gwh": j.act.groupby(key).sum() / 1000,
314	        # the two disjoint hour sets, each with its own forecast base so any window can
315	        # be expressed as a share rather than a bare volume
316	        "wind_fc_neg_gwh": j.fc.where(below, 0.0).groupby(key).sum() / 1000,
317	        "wind_def_neg_gwh": j.deficit.where(below, 0.0).groupby(key).sum() / 1000,
318	        "wind_fc_pos_gwh": j.fc.where(~below, 0.0).groupby(key).sum() / 1000,
319	        "wind_def_pos_gwh": j.deficit.where(~below, 0.0).groupby(key).sum() / 1000,
320	        "negative_price_hours": below.groupby(key).sum(),
321	    })
322	    return daily, adjacency(j, below)

325	def adjacency(j: pd.DataFrame, below: pd.Series, lags=(-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3)) -> dict:
326	    """The deficit as a share of forecast, by distance in hours from a negative price.
327	
328	    This is the test that identifies the effect, and it is the one the page was missing.
329	    A badly-forecast windy episode is smooth in time: it cannot produce a shortfall one
330	    hour wide. A price-triggered shutdown can, and does -- the deficit is around 9% of
331	    forecast in the negative hour and collapses to under 1% an hour either side.
332	
333	    Neighbouring hours that are themselves below zero are excluded from the lags, so the
334	    control is uncontaminated rather than quietly counting the same hours again.
335	    """
336	    idx = j.index
337	    pos = pd.Series(range(len(idx)), index=idx)
338	    neg_at = pos[below].to_numpy()
339	    prof = {}
340	    for k in lags:
341	        want = neg_at + k
342	        want = want[(want >= 0) & (want < len(idx))]
343	        rows = j.iloc[want]
344	        if k != 0:                                    # keep the control clean
345	            rows = rows[rows.px >= 0]
346	        if rows.empty or rows.fc.sum() <= 0:
347	            continue
348	        prof[str(k)] = {
349	            "hours": int(len(rows)),
350	            "share_of_forecast_pct": _n(rows.deficit.sum() / rows.fc.sum() * 100, 2),
351	            "deficit_gwh": _n(rows.deficit.sum() / 1000, 1),
352	        }
353	    # Per month over the same full record. The panel is range-independent, so its
354	    # seasonal caveat has to be too -- derived from whatever months the reader happened
355	    # to load, it credited July and never mentioned the April episode that carries the
356	    # result.
357	    neg = j[below]
358	    mk = neg.index.strftime("%Y-%m")
359	    by_month = []
360	    for m, g in neg.groupby(mk):
361	        if g.fc.sum() <= 0:
362	            continue
363	        by_month.append({
364	            "month": m,
365	            "hours": int(len(g)),
366	            "deficit_gwh": _n(g.deficit.sum() / 1000, 1),
367	            "forecast_gwh": _n(g.fc.sum() / 1000, 1),
368	            "share_of_forecast_pct": _n(g.deficit.sum() / g.fc.sum() * 100, 2),
369	        })
370	
371	    other = j[~below]
372	    return {
373	        # The broad control, answering a different question than the lags: is the
374	        # forecast simply biased low? It is not -- outside negative-price hours wind runs
375	        # slightly ABOVE forecast, so the deficit is not a general bias showing through.
376	        "control_other_hours": {
377	            "hours": int(len(other)),
378	            "deficit_gwh": _n(other.deficit.sum() / 1000, 1),
379	            "share_of_forecast_pct": _n(
380	                other.deficit.sum() / other.fc.sum() * 100, 2) if other.fc.sum() > 0 else None,
381	        },
382	        "note": ("Wind deficit against day-ahead forecast, as a share of that forecast, "
383	                 "by distance in hours from an hour whose day-ahead price was below "
384	                 "zero. Lag 0 is the negative hour itself; other lags exclude hours "
385	                 "that were themselves below zero, so they are a clean control. A "
386	                 "shortfall one hour wide cannot be forecast error. by_month covers the "
387	                 "negative-price hours only, over the same record."),
388	        "by_month": by_month,
389	        "negative_price_hours": int(below.sum()),
390	        "hours_total": int(len(j)),
391	        "covers": [str(idx[0].date()), str(idx[-1].date())],
392	        "profile": prof,
393	    }

423	def day_records(d: pd.DataFrame, source: str, flows: str,
424	                demand: pd.DataFrame | None = None,
425	                mv: pd.DataFrame | None = None,
426	                wind: pd.DataFrame | None = None) -> list[dict]:
427	    """One record per calendar day, with its per-border breakdown nested."""
428	    day = dtb.per_period(d, "day")
429	    per_bd = dtb.per_border_period(d, "day")
430	
431	    # the day's mean day-ahead price, deduplicated across borders first
432	    across = dtb._across_borders(d)
433	    px = across["price_de"]
434	    px = px.groupby(dtb.period_of(px.index, "day")).mean()
435	
436	    # Transit: in every hour Germany both imports and exports, and the overlap is
437	    # power that entered by one border and left by another. min() is the tight
438	    # bound on it and has to be taken per MTU -- min of daily totals would hide
439	    # every hour whose direction differed from the day's net.
440	    ov = across[["import_mwh", "export_mwh"]].min(axis=1)
441	    key = dtb.period_of(ov.index, "day")
442	    transit = ov.groupby(key).sum() / 1000
443	
444	    # The German price weighted by Germany's own share of the flows. Note what this
445	    # is and is not: it is the price the German zone cleared at during importing or
446	    # exporting hours, not a payment for imported energy -- nobody buys a labelled
447	    # imported MWh, everyone in the zone pays that hour's German price. Transit is
448	    # excluded because it is bought and sold in the same hour at the same price, so
449	    # leaving it in drags both averages together. Weighted per MTU, never an average
450	    # of daily averages.
451	    stayed = (across["import_mwh"] - ov)
452	    german = (across["export_mwh"] - ov)
453	    px_h = across["price_de"]              # hourly; `px` above is the daily mean
454	    def vw(vol):
455	        num = (vol * px_h).groupby(key).sum()
456	        den = vol.groupby(key).sum()
457	        return (num / den).where(den > 0)
458	    imp_px_own, exp_px_own = vw(stayed), vw(german)
459	    stayed_d = stayed.groupby(key).sum() / 1000
460	    german_d = german.groupby(key).sum() / 1000
461	
462	    out = []
463	    for date, r in day.iterrows():
464	        borders = {}
465	        if date in per_bd.index.get_level_values("day"):
466	            for border, b in per_bd.xs(date, level="day").iterrows():
467	                borders[border] = {
468	                    "import_gwh": _n(b["import_GWh"]),
469	                    "export_gwh": _n(b["export_GWh"]),
470	                    "net_import_gwh": _n(b["net_imp_GWh"]),
471	                    "bal_de_keur": _n(b["bal_de_kEUR"], 1),
472	                    "rent_keur": _n(b["rent_kEUR"], 1),
473	                    "mean_spread": _n(b["mean_spread"]),
474	                }
475	        dm = demand.loc[date] if demand is not None and date in demand.index else None
476	        mrow = mv.loc[date] if mv is not None and date in mv.index else None
477	        wrow = wind.loc[date] if wind is not None and date in wind.index else None
478	        out.append({
479	            "date": date,
480	            "source": source,
481	            "flows": flows,
482	            "price_de_mean": _n(px.get(date)),
483	            "load_gw": _n(dm["load_gw"]) if dm is not None else None,
484	            "residual_gw": _n(dm["residual_gw"]) if dm is not None else None,
485	            "import_gwh": _n(r["import_GWh"]),
486	            "export_gwh": _n(r["export_GWh"]),
487	            "net_import_gwh": _n(r["net_imp_GWh"]),
488	            "transit_gwh": _n(transit.get(date)),
489	            "stayed_gwh": _n(stayed_d.get(date)),
490	            "from_de_plants_gwh": _n(german_d.get(date)),
491	            "imp_px_own": _n(imp_px_own.get(date)),
492	            "exp_px_own": _n(exp_px_own.get(date)),
493	            "imp_px_de": _n(r["imp_px_de"]),
494	            "exp_px_de": _n(r["exp_px_de"]),
495	            "bal_de_keur": _n(r["bal_de_kEUR"], 1),
496	            "bal_zonal_keur": _n(r["bal_zonal_kEUR"], 1),
497	            "rent_keur": _n(r["rent_kEUR"], 1),
498	            "borders": borders,
499	            **({k: _n(v) for k, v in mrow.items()} if mrow is not None else {}),
500	            **({k: _n(v, 0 if k == "negative_price_hours" else 2)
501	                for k, v in wrow.items()} if wrow is not None else {}),
502	        })
503	    return out

506	def merge_months(outdir: str, fresh: list[dict], borders_asked: list) -> list[str]:
507	    """Upsert the fetched days into one file per calendar month, then reindex.
508	
509	    Monthly files rather than one growing store: the page only needs the months its
510	    selected range touches, and a single file would have the reader download every
511	    day ever recorded to look at the last week. Upsert still happens per date, so a
512	    re-fetch corrects days in place.
513	    """
514	    os.makedirs(outdir, exist_ok=True)
515	    by_month: dict[str, list[dict]] = {}
516	    for r in fresh:
517	        by_month.setdefault(r["date"][:7], []).append(r)
518	
519	    touched = []
520	    for month, rows in sorted(by_month.items()):
521	        path = os.path.join(outdir, f"{month}.json")
522	        try:
523	            with open(path) as fh:
524	                existing = {d["date"]: d for d in json.load(fh)["days"]}
525	        except (OSError, ValueError, KeyError):
526	            existing = {}
527	        added = sum(1 for r in rows if r["date"] not in existing)
528	        existing.update({r["date"]: r for r in rows})
529	        _write(path, {"month": month, "days": [existing[k] for k in sorted(existing)]})
530	        print(f"  {month}: {added} new, {len(rows) - added} updated, "
531	              f"{len(existing)} in file")
532	        touched.append(month)
533	
534	    reindex(outdir, borders_asked)
535	    return touched

542	    a range needs without downloading any of them.

## Snapshot System

The snapshot is your primary tool for understanding and interacting with pages.

```
-i        --interactive           Interactive elements only (buttons, links, inputs) with @e refs
-c        --compact               Compact (no empty structural nodes)
-d <N>    --depth                 Limit tree depth (0 = root only, default: unlimited)

-D        --diff                  Unified diff against previous snapshot (first call stores baseline)
-a        --annotate              Annotated screenshot with red overlay boxes and ref labels
-o <path> --output                Output path for annotated screenshot (default: <temp>/browse-annotated.png)
-C        --cursor-interactive    Cursor-interactive elements (@c refs — divs with pointer, onclick)
```

All flags can be combined freely. `-o` only applies when `-a` is also used.
Example: `$B snapshot -i -a -C -o /tmp/annotated.png`

@c refs from `-C` are numbered separately (@c1, @c2, ...).

# Refreshes the monthly files under data/ and publishes the dashboard.
#
# Pages is deployed from an artifact rather than from a branch folder, which is what
# frees the repo layout: index.html and data/ live at the root and the publish
# directory is assembled here from just those two. Set Settings -> Pages -> Source
# to "GitHub Actions" for this to work.
#
# Two things to know about the schedule:
#   * GitHub only fires `schedule` on the repository's DEFAULT branch. While this
#     lives on a side branch, the cron never runs; use workflow_dispatch, or make
#     this the default branch / merge it.
#   * It re-fetches the last few days rather than only yesterday, because both
#     sources revise recent days after first publication. Upsert is by date, so
#     re-fetching corrects a day in place instead of duplicating it.

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * *"        # 06:00 UTC, comfortably after D-1 is settled
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      date:
        description: "Start: YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY-MM or YYYY (blank = last 3 days)"
        required: false
      end:
        description: "End, inclusive (optional)"
        required: false

permissions:
  contents: write            # to commit the refreshed data
  pages: write               # to publish
  id-token: write            # required by deploy-pages

concurrency:
  group: daily-balance       # never let two runs race on the same files
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - run: pip install --quiet pandas requests

      # Uses build_data.py's default, SMARD, and deliberately takes no source
      # input: this job publishes, and SMARD is the only source that is both CC BY
      # 4.0 and gross per direction. ENTSO-E's prices (12.1.d) and scheduled
      # exchanges (12.1.f) are absent from its free-re-use list, so they are not
      # ours to redistribute; energy-charts is licensed but nets the flows away.
      # See the note at the top of build_data.py before changing this.
      - name: Fetch and merge
        # Inputs arrive as env vars, never interpolated into the script body --
        # `${{ inputs.date }}` inline would be a shell-injection hole.
        env:
          IN_DATE: ${{ inputs.date }}
          IN_END: ${{ inputs.end }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          if [ -n "$IN_DATE" ]; then
            if [ -n "$IN_END" ]; then
              python3 build_data.py --date "$IN_DATE" --end "$IN_END"
            else
              python3 build_data.py --date "$IN_DATE"
            fi
          else
            python3 build_data.py \
              --date "$(date -u -d '3 days ago' +%F)" \
              --end  "$(date -u -d 'yesterday' +%F)"
          fi

      - name: Commit if the data moved
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          git config user.name  "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git add data
          if git diff --staged --quiet; then
            echo "no change"
          else
            git commit -m "data: refresh through $(date -u +%F)"
            git push
          fi

      # Only what the page needs, so the scripts and git history are not published.
      # Locally the same layout works straight from the repo root -- see serve.py.
      - name: Assemble the site
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          mkdir -p _site
          cp index.html _site/
          cp -r data _site/data
          test -f _site/index.html && test -f _site/data/index.json
          du -sh _site

      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v5
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: _site

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
de_trade_balance.py -- Did Germany pay more for imported electricity than it
earned from exports, over a day or over a longer range?

Pulls, per border and per market time unit (MTU):
  * cross-border exchange DE-LU <-> neighbour, both directions
  * day-ahead price of DE-LU and of the neighbouring bidding zone

...then values the flows and prints a per-border summary plus a time series at
whatever resolution the range warrants (MTU, day, ISO week, month, year).

Data source: ENTSO-E Transparency Platform (https://transparency.entsoe.eu).
Requires a free API token: register, then Account Settings -> "Generate a new
token" (older accounts: email transparency@entsoe.eu asking for API access).

    export ENTSOE_API_TOKEN=...             # --source entsoe only
    pip install entsoe-py pandas requests
    ./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-08-16                    # one day, per MTU
    ./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-08-16 --source smard     # gross per direction
    ./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-07                       # all of July, per day
    ./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026 --by week                # the year, ISO weeks
    ./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-01-01 --end 2026-06-30 --by month
    ./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-08-16 --flows physical --csv out/
    ./de_trade_balance.py --demo                               # synthetic data


A NOTE ON WHAT "COST" MEANS HERE
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
There is no single true number, so this script reports three.

In the coupled European day-ahead market, cross-border trade is *implicit*:
nobody buys a labelled MWh "from France". Buyers in a zone pay their own zonal
price, sellers in a zone receive their own zonal price, and the algorithm moves
power across a border until either the prices converge or the interconnector
saturates. So for one MWh flowing X -> DE:

    German buyers pay          P_DE
    the seller in X receives   P_X
    the difference (P_DE-P_X)  is congestion rent, collected by the two TSOs
                               (normally split 50/50, and regulated back into
                               grid fees / interconnector investment)

Hence:

  balance_at_de_price   Everything valued at the German price. This is the
                        "what did this volume trade for at home" view and the
                        one journalism usually means. Under this metric, if DE
                        is a net importer in expensive hours and a net exporter
                        in cheap hours, the balance is negative.

                        Worth seeing that it collapses to
                        sum(net_MWh * price_de) per MTU: both directions carry
                        the same price, so gross volumes cancel and only the
                        net position in each hour survives. That makes it the
                        sturdiest of the three -- indifferent to whether the
                        source reports flows gross or already netted -- and it
                        is also why it says nothing about how much trade
                        actually took place.

  balance_at_zonal      Imports valued at the exporting zone's price, exports
                        valued at the German price -- i.e. money actually
                        leaving/entering the German market area, ignoring
                        congestion rent. Almost always the friendlier number.

  congestion_rent       Rent on both legs, which works out as
                        sum(net_MWh * spread) per border and MTU: imports earn
                        it when P_DE > P_X, exports when P_X > P_DE. Not a loss;
                        it is revenue to the two TSOs on that border, normally
                        split 50/50.

                        It is *not* the gap between the two balances above, easy
                        as that is to assume. balance_at_zonal only re-prices
                        the import leg -- exports sit at the German price in
                        both metrics -- so the gap is the import-side rent
                        alone: 43.6 of 99.6 MEUR over July 2026. The export-side
                        rent is real TSO revenue that neither balance reports.

                        Being net-only per border, it is as indifferent to gross
                        volumes as balance_at_de_price. entsoe and energy-charts

content.text:
Review done — I read the whole pipeline (`de_trade_balance.py` docstrings, `build_data.py`, `index.html`, the workflow) and ran the dashboard in a headless browser at desktop and mobile widths. Here's the full picture.

## What this is, and the verdict

A dependency-free static dashboard over a Python pipeline that values Germany's cross-border day-ahead flows per border and MTU, built on SMARD because it's the only source that is both CC-BY-licensed and gross-per-direction. The craft level is unusually high: the licensing analysis drives the architecture, the wind panel is built around an identification test rather than a headline number, sign-clipping bias in the old curtailment metric was found and documented, writes are atomic, the page is one file with hand-rolled SVG and a real dark mode. The main gaps are (a) one known data trap that the next cron run will actually spring, (b) a handful of small front-end bugs, and (c) a story that has outgrown its title — the strongest finding in the repo (the seasons disagree) isn't on the page at all.

## Technical findings

**1. The daily cron will quietly ruin the example-day panel.** `write_adjacency` guards against a narrow run overwriting a wide record, and its docstring names "the same trap `example_day` still has" — but it's still unfixed. The current `example_day.json` says "widest intraday price spread **on record**: 672 EUR/MWh" (2026-05-01), which the current code can no longer produce: it writes "widest … **in the refreshed range**", and the cron's range is the last 3 days. The first scheduled run replaces the most dramatic day of the year with whatever Tuesday was. Fix is the same guard: keep the file unless the new spread beats the recorded one (or recompute the spread from the month files already on disk, which needs no extra fetch).

**2. Sticky tooltip** (verified in the browser): hover any chart, scroll — the `position: fixed` tooltip stays at full opacity floating over unrelated panels until the pointer happens to leave a hit rect. On touch it's worse: a tap fires `pointerenter` and nothing ever dismisses it. One `scroll` listener calling `hideTip()` (and maybe a `pointerdown` outside) fixes both.

**3. Leftover dead code in `render()`** — `index.html:1557` computes `ownPx` and never uses it; `index.html:1569-1577` sets `volHint` via a ternary whose else-branch is immediately repeated in `if (!hasT)`, next to a `const _unused = netted;`. Clearly debris from the label-fix commit; worth sweeping before it confuses a future edit.

**4. Resolution: the analysis is hourly in a 15-minute market.** `align()` resamples everything to the `--freq` grid (default 60min) by mean, and the comment acknowledges day-ahead moved to 15-minute MTUs. For the balance and rent this is a small real error, not just smoothing — net position and price both vary within the hour, and the product of means isn't the mean of products. For the wind panel it's material: "hours priced below zero" misses quarter-hours below zero inside a positive-mean hour, and the panel's own § 51 EEG text explains that post-Feb-2025 plants respond to the *first negative quarter-hour* — a mechanism the hourly analysis literally cannot see. Running `build_data.py` at `--freq 15min` costs nothing on the published side (aggregation to daily happens in the pipeline) and would make the negative-hour counting match the market it describes.

**5. Small ones:** a failed month fetch inside a range-button click is an unhandled rejection — the button silently does nothing (worth an error surface). The month files ship six daily wind fields (`wind_fc_neg_gwh` etc.) the page never reads — fine if intentional as an audit trail, dead payload otherwise. The hero's `paid/earned` ratio would print nonsense if `earned` ever goes negative (possible in a deeply negative-price window).

## Presentation

What works: leading with the €127/MWh gap instead of the balance was the right reframe; the "three facts" card defuses the bad-faith reading before it starts; the red/blue money language is consistent everywhere including tooltips; transit as the neutral pole is a genuinely good encoding decision; the wind chart showing the *adjacency test* rather than a volume is the best panel on the page — the shape is the argument, as the caption says. Labels state their basis, the extreme bar is the only one labeled, and the table view backs everything.

What's weaker:

- **The headline claim is under-evidenced on screen.** The subtitle says the price "swings several-fold within a day," but the only intraday evidence is one fixed example day. Everything else is daily aggregates. An average day-profile for the selected window (price by hour-of-day, with the importing/exporting hours shaded red/blue) would directly connect the hero to the charts and prove the claim for *this* window, not one hand-of-god day.
- **"By border" is the orphan panel.** It's the only card with no takeaway sentence, the zone codes (DK1/NO2/SE4) are unexplained for anyone who isn't already in the field, and balance-only bars hide the difference between a quiet border and one with huge two-way churn that nets out. Even a hint line ("France is the biggest one-way supplier; the Netherlands mostly a corridor") would lift it to the standard of the rest.
- **The wind card is the text-heaviest thing on the page** — three dense paragraphs, one of which is a § 51 EEG commissioning-date taxonomy. The congestion card already shows the right pattern: headline + `<details>` for the law. Fold the who-stopped paragraph the same way.
